issues.legal_issue: A widow who has validly transferred property and later occupies it wrongfully does not acquire full ownership under the Hindu Succession Act merely because she remains in possession when the Act comes into force.
material_facts: The widow validly gifted the property to her daughter and the daughter took possession under the gift.
After the daughter’s death, the widow wrongfully retook possession from the daughter’s children and remained in possession when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
The widow had no right to possess the property when she retook it.
issues.conclusion: The widow’s later possession was that of a trespasser, not possession that could enlarge her interest under the Hindu Succession Act; she did not become the full owner.
issues.legal_principle: For property to be ‘possessed’ by a Hindu woman within section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, she must both have a right to possess it and be in actual or constructive possession. The Court relied on S. S. Munna Lal v. S. S. Rajkumar and Kuldip Singh v. Surain Singh. Because the widow lacked a right to possession, she acquired no ownership under the Act; the appellants’ reliance on section 14(2) did not alter that result.

predicates.claim_under_womens_property_succession_l: The dispute concerns whether a woman’s possession gives her an enlarged ownership interest under succession law.
predicates.valid_gift_and_delivery: The woman transferred the property by a valid gift and the donee took possession under it.
predicates.widow_reentered_wrongfully: The woman later retook possession without a right to do so.
predicates.widow_remained_in_possession_at_commence: The woman continued to occupy the property when the relevant succession law came into force.

issues.definition: When a woman claims enlarged ownership based on possession after a valid transfer, and she retook and held the property without a right to do so, she does not acquire full ownership.

issues.legal_issue: The special limitation rule for a tenant dispossessed from a tenancy holding does not govern a possession suit brought on the basis of a reversionary title that arose after the life interest ended.
material_facts: The claimant had earlier held the property as a tenant under a gift to the claimant’s mother and was dispossessed while that tenancy interest existed.
The claimant brought the suit after the widow’s death on the basis of a reversionary title, rather than as a tenant seeking recovery for the earlier dispossession.
The earlier dispossession was not the basis of the reversionary possession claim; that title arose on the widow’s death.
issues.conclusion: Section 104(1) and Article 1 of the Second Schedule to the C.P. Tenancy Act did not apply to the suit; limitation for the suit was governed by the Limitation Act, 1908.
issues.legal_principle: Section 104(1) and Article 1 of the Second Schedule to the C.P. Tenancy Act applied to a possession suit brought by a person claiming to be a tenant who had been dispossessed or excluded from possession. The claimant’s suit was instead based on a new title as reversioner arising after the widow’s death. The claimant’s earlier tenancy right could be extinguished under those provisions, but that did not make them applicable to the later reversionary claim.

rule.if: suit_for_possession and claim_based_on_reversionary_title and claim_arose_after_life_interest_ended and not suit_based_on_tenant_dispossession

predicates.suit_for_possession: The claimant seeks possession of property through a court proceeding.
predicates.claim_based_on_reversionary_title: The claimant bases the possession claim on a right to inherit after a life interest ends.
predicates.claim_arose_after_life_interest_ended: The claimant’s asserted reversionary right arose only when the life interest ended.
predicates.suit_based_on_tenant_dispossession: The claimant seeks possession in the capacity of a tenant on the ground of an earlier dispossession from the tenancy holding.

issues.definition: A possession suit based on a reversionary title arising after a life interest ends is not governed by the special limitation rule for suits based on a tenant’s dispossession.

issues.legal_issue: Wrongful possession of tenancy land does not give a trespasser a tenancy right against a prospective reversioner or extinguish that reversionary right before it accrues.
material_facts: The widow wrongfully possessed the tenancy property after retaking it from the donee’s children and continued in possession until her death.
The claimant’s earlier tenancy interest under the gift was distinct from the claimant’s prospective right as reversioner.
The claimant’s reversionary right arose only on the widow’s death, after the wrongful possession had continued beyond the period for a tenant’s recovery suit.
issues.conclusion: The widow acquired no right against the claimant as prospective reversioner through her wrongful possession, and the claimant’s reversionary right was not barred before it accrued.
issues.legal_principle: The C.P. Tenancy Act did not enable a trespasser to impose herself as a tenant by adverse possession, or to acquire a tenancy right affecting third parties through wrongful possession. The principle underlying section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908, is of general application, but a right cannot be barred before it accrues. The Court also considered Article 144 of that Act and explained that the claimant’s existing tenancy right and prospective reversionary right were distinct; only the former could be extinguished under the tenancy limitation provisions.

predicates.tenancy_holding_dispute: The dispute concerns land held under a tenancy.
predicates.wrongful_possession_continued_beyond_rec: A person remained in wrongful possession beyond the period available for recovery by the person then holding the tenancy interest.
predicates.claim_based_on_reversionary_title: The claimant bases the possession claim on a right to inherit after a life interest ends.
predicates.reversionary_right_accrued_after_possess: The claimant’s reversionary right arose only after the wrongful possessor had entered possession.

issues.definition: When wrongful possession of tenancy land continues beyond the recovery period but a claimant’s reversionary right arises only afterward, the possession gives the possessor no right against that claimant and does not extinguish the reversionary claim.
